Spider Webs

How is a spider web built, and how do its parts work together?

Where shall we look?

01Which lines are sticky on an orb web?↗02How can silk catch without glue?↗03How does a spider feel a tiny tug?↗04Why does dew make a web easy to see?↗

Which lines are sticky on an orb web?

Find the center hub, the straight lines that go out like spokes, and the spiral that winds around them.

A little explanation & something to try

On many orb webs, the spokes (radii) and the small hub are dry and strong. The outer spiral often holds tiny glue beads. Spiders walk the dry lines and feel prey on the sticky spiral. Not every web is an orb, and not every spiral is sticky the same way.

Try this. From a few steps away, sketch a web you can see. Mark the hub, three spokes, and one loop of the spiral. Do not touch the silk.

How can silk catch without glue?

Find the two silk samples: one with shiny droplets, and one that looks soft and woolly.

A little explanation & something to try

Some spiders make capture silk with glue droplets (ecribellate silk). Others comb out a dry, woolly silk with a special plate called a cribellum (cribellate silk). The woolly silk snags legs and wings without sticky glue. Scientists still study exactly how each kind works best.

Try this. On your sketch, label one spiral loop 'maybe glue' and write one question you still have about silk.

How does a spider feel a tiny tug?

Find the spider resting near the hub, with one or two legs on the silk.

A little explanation & something to try

Silk carries vibrations. Many spiders keep legs on the radii so a buzz or tug can travel to them. Tiny sensors in the legs help them tell a breeze from a struggling insect. They usually do not need sticky feet on every line because they know the dry paths.

Try this. Tap a table lightly with a pencil, then harder. Tell which tap felt bigger through your hand. That is only a toy model of vibration, not a real web.

Why does dew make a web easy to see?

Find the morning web with water beads shining on the spiral.

A little explanation & something to try

Cool mornings leave tiny water drops on silk. The drops catch light, so the web that was nearly invisible overnight suddenly shows its pattern. As the air warms, many drops shrink or fall. Dew helps us look; it is not glue from the spider.

Try this. On a cool morning, look for a web on a fence or bush. Count how many spiral loops you can see before the dew fades. Stay back and do not touch.

Spider webs, then deeper

Spider Webs

A web in the dew

Little Wonderer stopped on the path. "The bush is wearing lace," the little one whispered. Big Wonderer tipped its head. Overnight the web was almost invisible. Cool air left dew beads on the silk, and the beads caught the morning light. As the day warms, many drops shrink. Dew helps us see; it is not the spider's glue.

Why can a web be hard to see at night, then easy at dawn?

Hub, radii, spiral

Many orb webs share three parts. The hub is the small center. Radii are the straight spokes. The capture spiral winds around them. On many webs the radii stay dry and strong, while the spiral holds tiny glue beads. Spiders often walk the dry lines. Not every spider builds an orb, so what you find outside may look different.

Which parts of an orb web are often dry?

Silk that catches

Spiders make more than one silk. Dragline silk is strong for bridges and safety lines. Capture silk is for catching. Some spiders coat the spiral with glue droplets. Others comb out a dry, woolly silk with a cribellum plate. That woolly silk can snag without sticky glue. Researchers still compare how each kind works in wind and rain.

How can a web catch prey without sticky glue?

Feeling a tug

Big Wonderer watched the hub. A spider rested with legs on the radii. Silk carries vibrations, so a tiny tug can travel to those legs. Sensors help tell a breeze from prey. The spider usually does not need every line to be sticky, because it knows the dry paths home.

How can a spider notice prey without watching every second?

Look, don't touch

Little Wonderer lifted a pencil. Big Wonderer stayed a step back. A web is a home and a trap. Touching can break hours of work and may put a spider or a child too close. Sketch from a safe distance. Use eyes, a notebook, or a camera zoom. Leave the silk where it is.

Why should we look at webs without touching them?

Beads of light

Morning dew is water from the air, not spider glue. The drops sit on silk and sparkle, so the spiral pattern pops into view. Later the air warms and many beads shrink or fall. If you miss the dew, a soft side light may still reveal dry radii. Keep looking with care.

What makes dew different from the spider's sticky glue?

Quiz

1. Which orb-web parts are often dry?

2. How can silk catch without glue?

3. How does a spider feel a tiny tug?

4. What is morning dew on a web?

Answer key
Quiz 1
The hub and radii are often dry and strong; the spiral may hold glue.
Quiz 2
Woolly cribellate silk can snag legs and wings without glue droplets.
Quiz 3
Silk carries vibrations; legs on the radii can feel a tug that may mean prey.
Quiz 4
Dew is water from cool air. It catches light so the web pattern shows.

For grown-ups · Age 8

Look-don't-touch: watch webs from a step back. Outdoor dew walks are best on cool mornings. If anyone is afraid of spiders, keep the lesson on pictures and sketches. Hedge aloud with your child: many orb webs work this way, but spiders build other shapes too.

Age 8 with a stretch. Welcome spoken answers, pointing, drawing and dictation. Look-don't-touch outdoors.
